question: An intern is observing a fluoroscopy-guided procedure. Which combination of actions best reflects ALARA principles?

answers.text: Stand close to observe clearly, remove lead apron for comfort, and watch the full procedure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This violates all three ALARA practical methods: proximity maximises exposure, removing the apron removes shielding, and prolonged presence increases time. This is the most harmful approach.

answers.text: Stand at maximum feasible distance, wear a lead apron, and leave when not needed for learning

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Distance (inverse-square law), shielding (lead apron reduces trunk dose >90%), and minimising time in the field are the three practical ALARA methods applied together.

answers.text: Wear a lead apron but stand close to see the image better

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A lead apron provides shielding but proximity still increases scatter dose significantly. Distance is equally important as shielding.

answers.text: Ask the radiologist to stop the fluoroscopy beam whenever you are not actively watching

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While minimising beam-on time is good practice, an observer requesting beam stops disrupts the procedure. The intern's role is to manage their own position and time in the room.

overallFeedback.feedback: Not quite. The optimal approach combines all three ALARA practical methods: maximise distance (inverse-square law), wear a lead apron (shielding), and minimise time in the radiation field.
Correct! Maximum distance + lead apron + minimising time in the room combines all three ALARA practical tools simultaneously.
